list.listitem: Pubertal development in boys before the age of 9 years is precocious. C
Pubertal development in girls before the age of 8 years is precocious. C

Precocious puberty may be a sign of a serious underlying medical condition, potentially leading to reduced adult height and possible emotional or behavioral problems. The majority of patients, however, have benign, normal variations of puberty and do not require extensive evaluation. C

Treatment is directed at the underlying cause. In central precocious puberty, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists arrest further secondary sexual development and lead to increased adult stature. B

background.definition: Precocious puberty is the premature development of secondary sexual characteristics. In boys, sexual development before the age of 9 years is precocious. In girls, secondary sexual development before the age of 8 years is precocious.

list.listitem: Estimated at 0.01% to 0.05% per year in the United States.
It is significantly more common in girls than in boys.
Girls are more likely to have idiopathic sexual precocity, while boys are more likely to have underlying pathology.

The age of puberty onset has decreased over the past two centuries. Additionally, studies have found variations of menarche among different ethnic groups and a trend toward earlier puberty in girls with elevated BMI.

In central or complete precocious puberty, hypothalamic pulses of GnRH lead to increased gonadotropin (follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH] and luteinizing hormone [LH]) secretion and ultimately increased gonadal steroid (testosterone or estrogen) secretion. Central precocious puberty is linked with mutations in MKRN3.
In peripheral or GnRH-independent causes, autonomous secretion of gonadal steroids, gonadotropins, or hCG occurs without activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
Annual health supervision visits that include assessment of pubertal status are recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics. C
Assess pubertal development by physical examination using standard criteria (Tanner stages or Sexual Maturity Ratings). C
Gonadal steroid elevation with suppression of gonadotropins suggests autonomous secretion of gonadal steroids. C
Elevations in both gonadal steroids and gonadotropins imply that the etiology is gonadotropin dependent. C
Elevation in dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) for pubertal stage suggests adrenal pathology. C
Perform brain MRI in patients with central precocious puberty to rule out a CNS tumor or other serious lesion. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Isolated early breast development; patients usually younger than 3 years with no growth acceleration, minimally or nonprogressive
Early pubic hair, axillary hair, and/or axillary odor because of early adrenal androgen secretion; normal age of onset of other signs of puberty
Fat tissue rather than firm glandular breast tissue.
Isolated breast development; usually temporary and a variation of normal; may be pathologic in some cases
Early pubic and/or axillary hair, (+) family history; may be more severe than premature adrenarche
No other estrogen effects; menses cease, then normal puberty typically follows
Early development of secondary sexual characteristics due to increased production of gonadal steroids (may be GnRH dependent or independent)

list.listitem: When taking the history, elicit the type and duration of symptoms, the rate of pubertal progression, and whether a family history of early puberty is present. In reviewing the systems, address the possibility of an intracranial lesion.

In girls, precocious puberty presents as early glandular breast development. True glandular breast tissue must be distinguished from adipose tissue. Typically, glandular tissue overlies the areola and feels firmer and slightly more irregular than the surrounding adipose tissue.
In boys, precocious puberty presents as early testicular enlargement.
Isolated early pubic hair development without breast development (girls) or testicular enlargement (boys) is due to adrenal androgen production, not gonadal steroid production.

Signs of androgen effect, such as acne, axillary hair/odor, and clitoromegaly in girls, should be noted. Signs of estrogen effect, such as dulling of the vaginal mucosa in girls and gynecomastia in boys, should also be noted.
Evaluate height and growth velocity since increased levels of gonadal steroids lead to an early growth spurt and ultimately reduced adult height because of early epiphyseal closure.

Obtain serum gonadotropin and testosterone or estradiol levels (using specific pediatric assays for testosterone or estradiol and third-generation assays for FSH and LH). Gonadal steroid elevation with suppression of gonadotropins suggests autonomous secretion.
If early pubic hair is present, use DHEAS levels to evaluate adrenal androgen production. Elevated levels suggest premature adrenarche or adrenal pathology such as late onset CAH or adrenal tumor.
17-hydroxyprogesterone will be elevated in late-onset or non-classical CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Obtain a bone age in both boys and girls; advanced bone age will support a diagnosis of precocious puberty since elevated levels of gonadal steroids will cause skeletal maturation. However, the bone age will not be diagnostic of a specific disorder.

Obtain beta-hCG levels in boys with low gonadotropins and precocious puberty since elevated levels will interact with LH receptors and cause testosterone secretion. If levels are elevated, search for a beta-hCG-secreting tumor.

A meta-analysis of 6 studies found that urinary luteinizing hormone (ULH) had an AUC of 0.90 (sensitivity = 0.81, specificity = 0.85) for central precocious puberty in girls. The ratio of ULH to urinary follicle-stimulating hormone had an AUC of 0.8116 (sensitivity = 0.79, specificity = 0.84).
A diagnostic case control study found that a uterine artery pulsatility index > 4.6 combined with long axis uterine diameter <35 mm excludes female precocious puberty (AUROCC 0.94).
Order brain MRI in cases of complete or central precocious puberty to evaluate for possible CNS lesions.
A systematic review of case series found a pooled prevalence of intra-cranial abnormalities in children < 8 years old with central precocious puberty of 9%.
See algorithms in and for a suggested approach to evaluation in girls and boys, respectively.

A clinical decision rule can help identify girls with central precocious puberty who are at risk for occult intracranial lesions (OICLs). Age younger than 6 years is the strongest predictor of OICL in this study; other predictors used to achieve 100% sensitivity of detection in 7- to 8-year-old girls are the subject of controversy.
Treatment with GnRH agonists in central (GnRH-dependent) precocious puberty will arrest further secondary sexual development and lead to increased adult height. B
Treatment of incomplete precocious puberty is directed at the underlying etiology. C

Use GnRH agonists for idiopathic precocious puberty or precocious puberty because of a CNS lesion. Chronic administration of a GnRH analog leads to downregulation of GnRH receptors and a reduction of pituitary gland response to GnRH.
Intramuscular injections of depot forms every 4 weeks are safe, efficacious, and reversible.
Incomplete precocious puberty is GnRH independent; direct treatment at the underlying cause.

For patients with central precocious puberty, a network meta-analysis found that combined GnRH analogue and growth hormone led to the greatest final adult height compared with GnRH analogue alone or no therapy.
When a tumor is the cause of precocious puberty, surgical resection is indicated in many cases.
Adolescent gynecomastia that is severe and persistent may require surgical breast reduction.
Refer patients with precocious puberty to a pediatric endocrinologist.
Precocious puberty may indicate the presence of a serious underlying medical condition (such as a CNS neoplasm). C
Untreated precocious puberty leads to a reduction in final adult height. C
Psychological issues may arise for patients and their families. C
